newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-NEVADA TO CONSIDER PUNISHING TYSON FOR EAR BITING.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-NEVADA TO CONSIDER PUNISHING TYSON FOR EAR BITING.

text.p: With President Clinton declaring America was "horrified" at boxer Mike Tyson, an emergency meeting of the Nevada Athletic Commission Tuesday will ponder punishing Tyson for biting Evander Holyfield's ears in their World Boxing Association heavyweight title bout.
However, there will be no quick verdict. Tyson is entitled to a 30-day period in which to explain his actions in Saturday night's fight to the five-member panel that regulates boxing in the state.
But Tyson, on his 31st birthday, was taking an earlier opportunity for explaining himself to the world, scheduling a news conference for later on Monday.
Many in the sport have called for Tyson's boxing license to be revoked and for him to be banned for life from the sport. He was disqualified in the fight and suspended pending commission action.
The commission is under tremendous pressure to take strong action against Tyson while at the same time protecting the interests of boxing, an important industry in the economy of Nevada.

An internet company meanwhile announced plans for a class action lawsuit on behalf of people who paid to see the fight on cable television. "We paid for a Boxing Match, not a Biting Match," World Net Technologies said in a news release asking would-be litigants to sign up at www.usaworldnet.com.
Commission Chairman Elias Ghanem told the Las Vegas Review-Journal Monday that he favoured fining the fighter for the bites felt around the world.
"We would like to recommend holding all of the ($30 million) purse," said Ghanem. However, under state law, the commission may withhold only 10 percent of Tyson's pay from the fight.

The Nevada senate judiciary committee voted Sunday to change its rules and allow for seizure of 50 percent of the purse, but even if approved by the state legislature such rules could not be enacted retroactively.
Ghanem said that at Tuesday's meeting, the Commission would decide whether to file a complaint against Tyson and schedule a disciplinary hearing.
Bert Sugar, a revered boxing historian and writer, said Tyson had to be banned for life.
"If he is allowed to come back, it endorses his actions. Boxing doesn't need this," he told CBS television.
Boxing promoter Bob Arum called on the Commission to make an example of Tyson. "His conduct was obviously reprehensible and the Nevada Athletic Commission must take strong action," he told reporters.

"Boxing is too important to this state, a message has to be sent." Arum, however, is not exactly an objective observer. He is a bitter rival of Don King, who promoted the Tyson-Holyfield rematch on Saturday.

King himself has been unusually silent about the disqualification of the fighter he had billed as "the baddest man on the planet." Sources said King was unlikely to appear at Tuesday's Commission meeting.

Meanwhile, Dr Julio Garcia, who treated Holyfield at a local hospital after Saturday's fight, said the champion received 15 stitches for a wound that was about 1-1/2 inches (4 cm) wide on the top of his right ear. Holyfield who has returned home to Atlanta, will require reconstructive plastic surgery later.
His left ear was chewed up, but not damaged.
The injuries and how he received them sparked outrage, including from the White House. "I was horrified by it and I think the American people are," President Clinton said in a statement.
Tyson's troubles were not only confined to possible disciplinary action by boxing authorities.

The Las Vegas police and District Attorney's office were looking at videotape to determine if Tyson assaulted a police officer in the melee that erupted in the ring after he was disqualified just three rounds into the fight.

Metro Las Vegas police spokesman Sergeant Will Minor said it was up to individual officers to take legal action if they felt they were assaulted. However, it was unlikely such action would be taken, he said. The District Attorney, Stewart Bell, was not immediately available for comment Monday.

Judge Patricia Gifford, who presided over Tyson's 1992 rape trial in Indianapolis, said his probation was not likely to be affected -- unless criminal charges were filed. Tyson was released on four years' parole in March 1995 after three years in prison for the 1991 rape of a beauty pageant contestant.

In another development, police said there was no evidence of any shooting at the MGM Grand hotel/casino, where Saturday's fight took place. Sergent Minor said more than 40 people were injured in a stampede when reports of a shooting spread through the crowd after the bout in the world's largest casino.
